stops.name: San Francisco, the birth of Leonard Adleman
stops.date_confidence: attested exactly; the city is attested, the hospital and street are not named in any source reached
stops.campa: Leonard Max Adleman is born in San Francisco on the last day of 1945, to a bank teller and an appliance salesman. He will enter the University of California meaning to become a chemist and leave it a mathematician. Neither parent works in mathematics, and the trade he will help found does not exist yet: the machines that will run it are still being assembled out of vacuum tubes three thousand miles east, and the word cryptography still belongs to governments alone.

stops.name: Schenectady, the birth of Ronald Rivest
stops.date_confidence: attested exactly
stops.campa: Ronald Linn Rivest is born at Schenectady in upstate New York, a General Electric town, seventeen months after Adleman. He grows up in the suburb of Niskayuna and graduates from its high school in 1965. Three men whose initials will be spoken as one word for the rest of the century are born five thousand miles and seven years apart, into three families with no reason to know that the other two exist. The atlas records the distance first. The closeness comes later, and in one building.

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the birth of Adi Shamir
stops.date_confidence: attested exactly; city-centre coordinate, no address attested
stops.campa: Adi Shamir is born in Tel Aviv, four years into the state, the youngest of the three by five years and the only one born outside the United States. He will take all three of his degrees in Israel, cross to Massachusetts for a single stretch of four years, and then return to Rehovot and stay. Of the trio he is the one who leaves the country the algorithm is patented in, and the one who will spend the following decades taking other people's ciphers apart rather than building new ones.

stops.campa: Rivest takes a bachelor's degree in mathematics from Yale and leaves the east for California. He is twenty-two and has not yet met a cryptographer. What he has is the pure mathematician's training in structures that hold whether or not anyone is watching them. What he will build out of it is a lock whose key can be published on the front page of a newspaper without unlocking anything. The word for that object has not been coined and the object does not yet exist.

stops.campa: Shamir takes his first degree in mathematics from Tel Aviv University, in the city he was born in, and moves south to Rehovot for the rest of his training. He is twenty. The same year Rivest is finishing a doctorate at Stanford, and Adleman is midway through his own at Berkeley. Three trainings run in parallel across two continents with no contact between them and no common subject: an American algorithmist, an American number theorist, and an Israeli logician. All three will be finished within four years of each other, and within four years of that the three of them will be in one building.

stops.campa: Adleman teaches mathematics at MIT from 1976 to 1980, and here he meets Rivest, whose faculty appointment is in the department next door. The friendship precedes the problem. When Rivest starts bringing him constructions to check, Adleman checks them as a favour and as a game, the way a mathematician does, and finds the flaw in each one. Nobody yet calls this cryptanalysis. It is two colleagues arguing over a blackboard, and it goes on through the winter.

stops.name: Stanford, New Directions in Cryptography
stops.date_confidence: publication month attested; day is a default. Pin inherited byte-identical from hellman.journey.json
stops.campa: Diffie and Hellman publish New Directions in Cryptography in the IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, describing a cipher whose encryption key can be made public, and admitting they have no construction for one. The paper travels three thousand miles east and lands on Rivest's desk. What Stanford has posed as a possibility, MIT reads as an assignment. The arithmetic both parties reach for is modular exponentiation, which Gauss set down in the Disquisitiones Arithmeticae in 1801 and which the atlas already holds.
stops.quote: This method provides an implementation of a "public-key cryptosystem," an elegant concept invented by Diffie and Hellman. Their article motivated our research, since they presented the concept but not any practical implementation of such a system.

stops.name: 545 Technology Square, the paper read and the functions broken
stops.date_confidence: the reading of Diffie and Hellman is attested; the month is a reconstruction from the publication date and the April 1977 result, and the day is a default
stops.campa: At the Laboratory for Computer Science, in the Technology Square building, Rivest and Adleman divide the work without agreeing to divide it. Rivest proposes candidate one way functions; Adleman breaks them. Accounts vary on how many, and the figure commonly repeated is forty-two, which no participant is on record as confirming. Shamir joins them and proposes his own, which Adleman also breaks. The method is not deduction. It is a man building locks in front of another man whose entire pleasure is picking them.
stops.quote: Our encryption function is the only candidate for a "trap-door one-way permutation" known to the authors.
stops.quote_source: Rivest, Shamir, Adleman, 'A Method for Obtaining Digital Signatures and Public-Key Cryptosystems', Communications of the ACM 21(2), February 1978, Section XI, Conclusions, p. 133

stops.campa: Unable to sleep, Rivest lies down with a mathematics textbook and works through the night on a function built from the product of two large primes, easy to compute in one direction and, so far as anyone knows, hopeless in the other. He telephones Adleman before dawn. Adleman attacks it and cannot break it. By daybreak most of a paper exists. Adleman asks to have his name taken off it, on the grounds that the invention is not his; Rivest refuses, and Adleman settles for being listed third.

stops.campa: The first written account of the method is issued from the Laboratory for Computer Science as technical memorandum MIT LCS TM-82, titled On Digital Signatures and Public-Key Crypto-Systems. It is not sent to a funder for approval and it is not a journal submission. It is mailed free to anyone who posts Rivest a self-addressed envelope. Some accounts describe it as a report submitted to the Office of Naval Research, which funded the underlying work; the navy was a payer, not an addressee.

stops.name: 545 Technology Square, the method in Communications of the ACM
stops.date_confidence: issue month attested; day is a default. The manuscript is stamped received 4 April 1977 and revised 1 September 1977
stops.campa: A Method for Obtaining Digital Signatures and Public-Key Cryptosystems appears in Communications of the ACM, seven pages that give the algorithm its permanent name and its permanent shape. The abstract opens on the property that makes it strange: the key can be published. The paper credits Diffie and Hellman by name for the concept in its first section, thanks Hellman in its acknowledgments, and invites the reader to attack it. Xerox PARC lent the text editing machines that set the final manuscript.
stops.quote: An encryption method is presented with the novel property that publicly revealing an encryption key does not thereby reveal the corresponding decryption key.

stops.campa: Shamir, still at MIT, publishes How to Share a Secret: a secret is encoded as a polynomial, each holder is given one point on it, and any sufficient number of them together recover the curve while any smaller number learns nothing at all. Two men arrive at threshold secret sharing at once, as three men arrived at public keys inside four years.

stops.date_confidence: Fred Cohen's own account dates the conception to 3 November 1983 and the demonstration to the weekly security seminar on 10 November 1983. Some retellings misplace the demonstration at Lehigh University; Cohen was Adleman's doctoral student at USC and both men place it there
stops.campa: Fred Cohen, a doctoral student of Adleman's, demonstrates a self-replicating program to the weekly computer security seminar. Adleman, who is at the same time running experiments on HIV in a molecular biology laboratory across the campus, hears the description and supplies the analogy from the work on his other bench. The name sticks to the thing permanently. One of the three men who made secure communication possible also named the sickness that would travel along it.
stops.quote: somewhere along the line during our discussions I started calling these things computer viruses.

stops.name: Santa Barbara, the Fiat-Shamir scheme
stops.date_confidence: conference year attested; CRYPTO is held in August, and the month is inferred from the conference's regular schedule, the day a default
stops.campa: At the CRYPTO conference on the Santa Barbara campus, Amos Fiat and Shamir present How to Prove Yourself, a method by which one party convinces another that it holds a secret without disclosing any part of the secret. The trick of turning that interaction into a signature by replacing the verifier with a hash function will still be in daily use forty years later, under their two names. Shamir now has three permanent inventions and only the first of them is shared.

stops.name: Santa Barbara, differential cryptanalysis
stops.date_confidence: presented at CRYPTO '90 in August 1990; the journal version follows in the Journal of Cryptology in 1991. Day is a default
stops.campa: Eli Biham and Shamir present Differential Cryptanalysis of DES-like Cryptosystems, the first published general method for attacking a block cipher by feeding it chosen pairs of inputs and watching how the difference between them propagates. It works on almost every cipher then in use except the Data Encryption Standard, whose designers, it emerges, had known about the attack in 1974 and had quietly built the standard to resist it. The open literature has caught up with the closed one by sixteen years.
suggested_refs: Biham and Shamir, 'Differential Cryptanalysis of DES-like Cryptosystems', CRYPTO '90

stops.name: San Francisco, the first RSA Conference
stops.date_confidence: founding year attested; month and day are defaults. The Moscone Center coordinate is the venue of the conference's later decades, not of the first meeting of about fifty people
stops.campa: Jim Bidzos gathers roughly fifty cryptographers to argue about standards, and the meeting becomes annual. It grows into the largest security gathering in the world, tens of thousands of people in the Moscone halls, named after an algorithm three academics wrote in a Cambridge spring. The men whose initials are on the banner are not the organisers of it. The same year RSA Laboratories opens the Factoring Challenge, with prizes up to two hundred thousand dollars for anyone who can undo the arithmetic.
stops.quote: The security of the system rests in part on the difficulty of factoring the published divisor, n.
stops.quote_source: Rivest, Shamir, Adleman, 'A Method for Obtaining Digital Signatures and Public-Key Cryptosystems', Communications of the ACM 21(2), February 1978, p. 120, abstract

stops.name: Morristown, the magic words
stops.date_confidence: the factorisation completed 26 April 1994. The Bellcore coordinate is the coordinating site; the computation itself ran on some 1,600 machines operated by more than 600 volunteers on four continents and has no single place
stops.campa: Eight months of donated machine time, coordinated by Derek Atkins, Michael Graff, Arjen Lenstra, and Paul Leyland, finish the number Gardner printed seventeen years earlier. The estimate offered in 1977 was on the order of forty quadrillion years. The plaintext, chosen by Rivest as a phrase no dictionary attack would guess, comes out of the arithmetic intact. The method has not failed. Its safety is a quantity, measured in digits, and the quantity has to keep going up.
stops.quote: THE MAGIC WORDS ARE SQUEAMISH OSSIFRAGE
stops.quote_source: The plaintext of the RSA-129 challenge cipher set by Rivest and published in Martin Gardner's Scientific American column, August 1977; recovered by Atkins, Graff, Lenstra, and Leyland, April 1994
suggested_refs: Atkins, Graff, Lenstra, and Leyland, 'The Magic Words are Squeamish Ossifrage' (1994)

stops.name: Los Angeles, the Hamiltonian path in a test tube
stops.date_confidence: publication date of the Science paper, vol. 266, pp. 1021 to 1024
stops.campa: Adleman publishes Molecular Computation of Solutions to Combinatorial Problems in Science: a seven-node Hamiltonian path problem solved by strands of DNA in a tube, the answer selected out of the soup by the chemistry of base pairing rather than computed by any processor. He founds a second field at forty-eight. The man who once broke Rivest's constructions for the pleasure of it spends his second career proving that computation does not require a computer, on a bench beside the one where he was culturing virus.

stops.name: Cheltenham, the prior claim declassified
stops.date_confidence: the 1997 declassification is attested and the internal document is dated 1973; month and day are defaults. Pin inherited byte-identical from hellman.journey.json
stops.campa: British signals intelligence releases a note written at Cheltenham in 1973 by a mathematician named Clifford Cocks, A Note on Non-Secret Encryption, describing the same construction four years before Cambridge. It had been classified for twenty-four years. Had it been known, the American patent would have been invalid on its face. The atlas has been to this coordinate for Diffie and Hellman, whose priority the same release also displaced. Two open discoveries turn out to have been made twice, and the earlier making was silent.

stops.name: Bedford, the patent released early
stops.date_confidence: attested exactly; the patent's own expiry was 20 September 2000
stops.campa: RSA Security puts the algorithm into the public domain a fortnight before the patent would have lapsed of its own accord, ending the licensing requirement two weeks early and gaining the gesture rather than the fortnight. From this date the method belongs to everyone. It is by then the arithmetic underneath a large fraction of the commerce conducted on the internet, and the twenty-three years of monopoly it enjoyed applied in exactly one country, the one whose patent office granted it.

stops.name: San Francisco, the Turing Award and the three laws
stops.date_confidence: the award is for 2002 and was presented at the ACM Awards Banquet in June 2003 per the AMS Notices of July 2003; a contemporaneous report of Shamir's Turing lecture dates the lecture to June 2002. stops.campa: The Association for Computing Machinery gives the three of them one Turing Award, for their ingenious contribution for making public-key cryptography useful in practice. Shamir uses his lecture to state three laws of security, of which the third is the one people repeat. Thirteen years later the same association gives the same award to Diffie and Hellman for the paper that started them. The second of the two prizes goes to the men who had the idea first.

stops.name: Takoma Park, the ballot that can be checked
stops.date_confidence: election date attested. Rivest's specific role in the deployment is reported by the USENIX Security 2010 paper on the election; the extent of his personal presence in Takoma Park is not attested and is not claimed here
stops.campa: Scantegrity II, an end-to-end verifiable ballot system designed by Rivest with David Chaum and others, runs a binding municipal election in a Maryland town of seventeen thousand, the first governmental use of a system in which a voter can confirm that their own vote was counted without being able to prove to anyone else how they cast it. It is used again in 2011. The late work of the man who made secrecy computable is a machine for making a secret checkable.

stops.name: MIT Stata Center, the Institute Professorship
stops.date_confidence: announced June 2015, effective the following July; day is a default. The laboratory left Technology Square for the Stata Center in 2004
stops.campa: MIT names Rivest an Institute Professor, the highest rank the university confers and one held by fewer than thirty people in its history. He has been on this faculty for forty-one years. The laboratory itself moved out of the Technology Square building in 2004 and into the Stata Center, four hundred metres from where the seder night's arithmetic was written up, so the address changes and the walk does not. He is still working on cryptography and on how to count votes.

stops.name: San Francisco, the panel on cryptocurrencies
stops.date_confidence: attested exactly; the panel was held Tuesday 29 April 2025 at the RSA Conference and reported the same week by Decrypt and The Register. Part of the gathered material dated this remark 2022, which is wrong
stops.campa: At the conference that carries his initials, seventy-two years old, Shamir sits on a panel and says what he thinks of the industry that took his arithmetic furthest. He adds that nobody uses it to make payments, that people buy it once in order to speculate, and that everything is highly centralised in a small number of very large exchanges. The hall is named for the algorithm, and the audience in it works in a trade the algorithm made possible. The man saying this broke more ciphers than he built.
stops.quote: My personal opinion is that the world would have been better without cryptocurrencies.

stops.name: Cambridge, Rehovot, Los Angeles: three addresses and no tomb
stops.date_confidence: status at the time of research, August 2026; the date is the atlas convention for living subjects. The coordinate is the canonical MIT pin, standing for the only address the three of them ever shared
stops.campa: All three are alive as this journey is written. Rivest is an Institute Professor at MIT, Shamir is at the Weizmann Institute, Adleman retired from the University of Southern California in 2016 as professor emeritus. There is no grave to visit and no plaque was found for the night in April 1977; no source reached names a marker, a room, or a house. The monument is a computation performed some billions of times a day by machines that do not know whose it is. The absence of a stone is set down here as an absence.
